samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers diagnose the drift well and quote specific values. A is stronger because it gives concrete target scales for spacing, radius and type, orders the migration by blast radius with reasons, and states which merges will visibly shift layouts. B only describes token counts without values, says near-duplicates collapse "without anyone noticing", and both answers assert that inputs and selects sit side by side, which the CSS doesn't show. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers spot the same near-duplicate colours, radii, spacing and shadows, and quote the specific values. B is stronger because it proposes concrete scales and roles (spacing 4–48, radius by control/container/overlay, two elevation levels). It also orders the migration by blast radius and says which changes will be visible, while A only gives counts of tokens. B also states its assumptions openly, and keeping the overlay elevation and radius separate shows it isn't flattening differences that may be intentional.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find the same near-duplicates and give a similar plan based on tokens and a stylelint rule. B is more accurate and more careful: it quotes every value correctly, starts with a usage audit so the merges are based on evidence, and avoids unsupported claims. A miscounts the padding values (it says 7 but lists 8), says the values were copied from mockups without evidence, and guesses that the greys fail contrast, though it does add a caveat. A does handle the modal's elevation as intentional a little more explicitly. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers quote the specific near-duplicate values well. A gives a more concise, better-justified order: audit usage counts first, then pick scales, then define tokens, then migrate component by component. B is stronger at separating intentional differences, since it explicitly keeps the modal's overlay shadow as its own level, and it states its assumptions more clearly. However, B is wordier, miscounts the paddings (says 7, lists 8), makes unsupported claims about contrast and mockup origins, and its reasoning for doing spacing last is muddled.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A is more concrete. Its old-to-new mapping tables cover color roles, radius, shadow, spacing, type and control height. It treats the modal shadow as a deliberate overlay level rather than flattening it. Its order of define tokens, add them without visual change, then migrate is well justified. B is tighter and also well ordered, but its target values are vaguer, it does less to separate intentional from accidental differences, and it states the contrast failure more confidently. A loses points for length, extra material on governance and dark mode, and a leftover placeholder. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B is the stronger answer. It turns the drift into a concrete old-to-new token mapping, keeps the modal's higher shadow as a deliberate `shadow.overlay` while merging the accidental duplicates, and adds tokens without visible change before migrating, with a reason for each step's order. A finds the same near-duplicates and is tighter, but it says to snap everything to tokens without separating intentional differences from accidents, and it gives few concrete color or spacing targets. Both make contrast claims they haven't checked, though B hedges and says to verify with a tool; B also wanders into component states, governance and dark mode.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers bury a coherent token set under long lists of additions, which works against the rubric's call for few changes and brevity. Answer A is shorter, but it asserts that contrast is solid before admitting the ratios were hand-estimated, and it calls a z-index scale and --radius-lg cheap to add now. Answer B is longer, but it names why the set is coherent, flags its contrast estimates up front, and pushes back on speculative growth: no filling in spacing steps, --radius-lg only when needed, no raw color ramp yet. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers affirm the set is sound but then pile on many additions (focus, strong border, status tints, fonts, touch targets, motion, and more). Neither stays short, though both avoid renaming tokens or reprinting the file. A edges ahead: it flags its contrast estimates as approximate up front, explicitly warns against filling scale gaps or adding a primitive ramp, and adds fewer speculative tokens. B adds more speculative scales (text-xs, z-index, radius-lg, action-active, row hover/selected), states a WCAG failure and an unverified hex value as fact, and only hedges about contrast at the end.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers open by calling the set coherent, but then list a long run of additions, which works against the rubric's few-changes, keep-it-short goal. B is somewhat better. It praises the existing design specifically, says up front that its contrast figures are estimates to verify, and ties additions such as touch targets to the warehouse use case. A states the border contrast failures as fact and piles on more speculative tokens (z-index, breakpoints, extra spacing steps, more easings, surface tiers). | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers open by calling the set coherent, but both then suggest far more additions than a sanity pass needs. A is a bit leaner, ties most additions to real warehouse needs (control borders, focus, touch targets, tabular numbers), and treats contrast figures as estimates to verify. B adds more speculative tokens (z-index, breakpoints, extra easings, more spacing steps, a mono font, hover-row colors) and states the border's WCAG failure as fact before hedging later.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers over-reach. Each proposes a dozen or more new tokens for a set that is already coherent, and neither treats v1 as mostly ready to ship. B does better on hedging: it says its contrast numbers need checking and lists what to leave alone. But it is much longer, includes a large patch, and suggests a namespace prefix, which would rename every token. A is shorter and leads with a verdict, but it states its contrast figures as fact. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Neither answer accepts that the set is basically ready. Both turn the review into a long list of additions, so both fall short on restraint. B wins narrowly because it is shorter and adds no patch full of speculative tokens, though it states contrast results as fact where A correctly marks them as estimates to verify. A has a clear 'leave alone' section and keeps the existing naming, but its six must-fix items, five more suggestions and a full starter patch go well beyond small, justified gaps.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick a 4px base with about a 1.2 ratio, connect that choice to dense table rows and gloved touch targets, and handle density with separate modes chosen by device rather than viewport width. B treats Tailwind better by turning the tokens into the only allowed Tailwind config values, and it trims its spacing steps more deliberately. However, it hedges with '1.125–1.2' and 'merge them if too close', and it runs noticeably longer. A commits more firmly and is shorter, while still giving a developer enough to implement. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both pick a 4px base with about a 1.2 ratio, and both handle the desktop/tablet conflict with density modes and 48–56px glove targets. A has more deliberate spacing steps (it leaves out 20 and 40) and a more practical Tailwind plan, but it hedges the ratio as 1.125–1.2 and runs longer. B commits more cleanly, stays tighter, and adds useful details such as gaps between adjacent targets and pointer: coarse detection, though its spacing list is a little less curated.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers choose a 4px base with a 1.2 ratio, connect the choice to dense tables and gloved touch use, and treat Tailwind fairly as tooling to override. B is better: its spacing scale has 8 deliberate steps instead of A's 12, one shared type ladder shifts up a step for touch mode, and it is tighter overall. B's flaws are minor: 6px compact cell padding is off the 4px grid, and its rounded ladder is loosely derived from 1.2. A gets credit for three density modes and its CSS-variable implementation tip, but its 13px tablet xs size undercuts its own advice not to go below 16px on tablet. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers commit to the 4px base with a 1.2 ratio and tie the choice to dense tables and gloved tablet use, with explicit density modes and minimum tap targets. A is tighter: it uses 8 deliberate spacing steps and a short, rounded type ladder where touch mode moves each role up one step. B allows 12 spacing steps, includes odd sizes such as 13, 17, 19, 23 and 33px, and is longer, though its Tailwind guidance (CSS variables on a data-density attribute) is slightly more useful.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers choose a 4px base with a 1.2 ratio and handle Tailwind fairly, but B's numbers hold together better. Its 1.2 type scale is consistent and its density table adds up (4+20+4 = 28 fits a 32px row, 16+24+16 = 56). B also covers the space between gloved targets, how to switch density, and tabular numerals. A's compact mode has a mistake: 8px vertical padding around a 20px line is 36px, which doesn't fit its 32px row. Its 12/14 sizes also don't follow the 1.2 ratio it claims. A is a bit shorter. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers choose a 4px base with a 1.2 ratio and handle Tailwind fairly, but A's density table is more complete. It sets explicit gaps between targets for gloved use, picks the default mode with pointer: coarse and gives button heights for each mode. B labels its scale a 1.2 ratio, but its 12/14 sizes don't follow that ratio from 16. Its compact row also doesn't add up: 8px vertical padding plus a 20px line height won't fit in 32px. Both answers cite a 20px step that neither spacing scale includes.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A has the tighter shared system. A single content/wide/full grid and one spacing token serve both docs and marketing, there are only three breakpoints, and the shell stops growing at a clear 1440px cap. It has small flaws: the 4/8-column scheme in its table is never implemented, and 52ch appears as a literal number even though a matching token exists. Answer B handles code and tables more thoroughly, including bleeding them to the screen edge on phones, but its CSS is messier: a duplicated `.pricing` block with a `composes` line that only works in CSS modules, repeated magic numbers (34rem, 4rem, 28rem), a fourth breakpoint, and root-font scaling that keeps the page growing on very large monitors. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B uses one content/wide/full grid that serves both articles and marketing. Code and tables break out to the wide track and scroll, and it gets by with three breakpoints and a clear 1440px cap. A is thorough, with good phone bleed and min-width fixes, but its CSS has an invalid `composes` line, defines the pricing grid twice, and repeats magic values like 4rem and 34rem. Its root-font bump on very wide screens also partly undercuts the stop-growing goal. B has small lapses of its own: 52ch and 16.25rem are hard-coded rather than tokenized, and the 4/8/12 columns in its table are never implemented, but it is cleaner overall.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both give plausible numbers, cap growth on big monitors and make code and tables scroll inside their own box. B keeps docs and marketing on one clearly tokenized set of widths (measure, content, wide, docs-main), and its explicit pricing column counts avoid orphaned cards. A has the richer table handling, including the sticky first column, but it repeats literal values such as 90rem, 72rem and 17rem instead of using its tokens, and it lists a 40rem breakpoint it never uses. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give plausible values and a named-line grid with prose, wide and full tracks, and both have code and tables scroll inside their own box. A is more disciplined: nearly every width is a named token, the docs shell width is built from those tokens, and the pricing grid avoids a lone card on its own row. B hard-codes 72rem and 90rem even though it defines --page-max, and it adds extras like heading sizes and sticky table columns. B's notes on mid-size docs columns and big monitors are useful, but its auto-fit pricing grid can leave a lone card on the last row.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B has a smaller set of named tokens (prose, wide and page widths, plus margin and gap), exactly three breakpoints, and one named-line grid that both docs and marketing pages use, which matches the 'one set of rules' request well. A is thorough and handles viewport sizes in more detail, including wide monitors and a container-queried pricing grid. However, A uses five breakpoints plus container queries and a font-size ramp, repeats literals like 4.5rem, 55ch and 15rem, and has a selector bug: it hides `aside` but the sidebar is a `nav`, so the sidebar is never hidden on phones. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give plausible numbers, separate the prose column from the wider marketing grids, and scroll code and tables inside their own boxes. A is tighter: one named-line grid serves both kinds of page, it uses three breakpoints, and it reuses its named values consistently. B adds extra breakpoints, scales the font and page width on big monitors, and sprinkles in values like 55ch, 20ch and 1.1fr. B does have good touches: container-query pricing and keyboard access to scrolling tables (tabindex).

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A is narrowly better: its message reads as one consistent process, and it pastes with fewer edits (an invented but plausible channel, disclosed afterward) than B, which has a 'Here's the message:' preamble and bracketed placeholders. B has stronger semantic examples and a sharper rule for when to add a token ('a second screen or team needs it'). But B says to keep one-offs local as exceptions, then says 'no new one-off values in PRs,' which contradicts itself. Both stay well under 120 words, and both add notes after the message. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both drafts stay under 120 words. A's naming examples are more consistently role-based, and it tells people outright to reuse the nearest token. It also gives a clear test for adding one: a second screen or team needs it. B names approvers and a review cadence, but its `space-4`/`space-8` examples are named by value, which undercuts its 'purpose, not value' rule, and it never tells people to use the closest existing token. B is cleaner to paste because it has no preamble, though both add a note after the message.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both messages fit the word limit, but both wrap the paste-ready text in a preamble and closing notes, which costs them on item 1. A wins narrowly: it names an owner (design and eng) and a review window, and its tone stays friendly. B opens with 'Please stop adding one-off colors,' which reads as scolding. B has the stronger purpose-based examples and a good test for additions ('a second screen or team needs it'), but it has no approver, and A's 'space-4' and 'radius-md' weaken its own naming rule a little. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers wrap the message in a preamble and trailing notes, but each message is under 120 words. A has the more consistent role-based naming and a useful test for additions (a second screen or team needs it). However, its opening 'Please stop adding one-off colors' reads as scolding, and it names no approver. B is friendlier, names who reviews (design and eng) and how fast (2 business days), and still says to check existing tokens first, though its `space-4` example breaks its own name-by-purpose rule.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B's message has a firmer test for new tokens: name the existing token you tried, explain why it doesn't fit, and show two screens that need the new one. It also says plainly that near-miss values get merged into the existing token, and its placeholders mark exactly what the team must fill in. A also works and openly says its details are invented, but it opens with a slightly scolding 'Please stop,' gives weaker reuse guidance, and its 'space-4' example names a value on the spacing scale rather than a purpose. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A explicitly says to reuse the closest existing token, using the near-miss hex example. Its process has a real test: name the token you tried and show two screens that need the new one. Its tone is firm but not scolding. B opens with "Please stop adding one-off colors," which reads as a reprimand, includes the value-based `space-4` despite its purpose-not-value rule, and only implies the reuse step.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep every computed value and class name, and both handle the secondary button's border with calc() in the same way. B names spacing by step (space-1 to space-6) rather than by pixel value, and it explains why it left the close steps (12/14 and 18/20) unmerged. A names spacing by pixel value and only notes that it could be renamed later. B loses a little for unprompted remarks about dark mode and missing states, and its summary is slightly longer. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers keep every computed value and class name the same, and both handle the secondary button's padding with a calc() of the shared tokens, so the two buttons stay the same size. A names its spacing tokens as scale steps (space-1 to space-6) and explains why it left the close values 12/14 and 18/20 unmerged. B names its spacing tokens by pixel value (--space-10), which goes against the rubric's role-or-step naming, though B admits this trade-off. Both summaries are short; B's note on reordering properties is harmless but adds churn, and A's mention of theming is only a remark, not built code.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep every class name and computed value, and both derive the secondary button's 9px/17px padding with calc so the two buttons stay the same size. A names its tokens by role, adds a border-width token so the calc and the borders share one value, and gives a short, useful summary. B adds a palette layer named by appearance (teal-700, slate-200) underneath the role names and points toward theming, which the request didn't ask for. B's merge map is helpful, but its notes run longer. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers keep every rendered value and class name exactly as they were, and both derive the secondary button's 9px/17px padding with calc so the two buttons stay the same size. A adds a raw palette tier named by appearance (teal-700, slate-200) beneath the role names and pitches it as groundwork for a dark theme or second brand, which goes beyond the request. B uses one tier of role-named tokens, adds a border-width token, and gives a short, focused list of things to check.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A does more of what the request is about: it turns spacing, font sizes, weights, radii, colors and motion into tokens, with role-based names that components use. It also correctly keeps 12/14 and 18/20 as separate values and explains the 2px shift that merging them would cause. B is leaner and its summary is clearer, but it leaves spacing and font sizes as literals, which fits the request less well. A loses points for an unrequested raw-plus-semantic token layer, for dropping `.btn-danger`'s white text color, and for a confusing note about `border:0`. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Answer A keeps every computed value identical, derives the secondary button's padding from the border width with calc, and stays lean. Its weak spot is leaving spacing and font sizes as literals, saying they don't repeat, when 10px, 14px and 18px do. Answer B tokenizes much more thoroughly and explains the snapping trade-offs well, but it adds a raw-palette layer and dark-theme framing nobody asked for. B also drops `color:#fff` from `.btn-danger`, which could change a combined `.btn-secondary.btn-danger`, and its note about `border:0` being inherited is wrong.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are well built and very similar: matching light themes, a dark theme with lifted greens and coral reds that read well on a dark surface, and a high-contrast theme with bolder borders, a darker button, and +/− signs on amounts. A is slightly stronger. Its high-contrast red is deeper and easier to read, and its sample screen is richer, with in/out totals and transaction categories. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers look almost the same: the light theme matches the brief, the dark palette uses lighter greens and coral on near-black, and the high-contrast theme has darker colors and heavy rules. B is slightly stronger in high contrast, with an outlined button and stronger borders, and it adds category labels and an arrow icon next to the signs. B also says on the page that the themes only remap semantic roles. In both answers the thicker high-contrast borders make that card a little taller than the others. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): The two answers are very similar: both show a well-tuned light theme, a considered dark palette with lighter green and salmon tones, and a high-contrast theme with darker tones, black borders and +/− signs. A's high-contrast theme is a bit stronger because the action button has a heavy border and the balance change has an arrow icon. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers keep radius at zero, show depth with rules and zero-blur offsets instead of soft shadows, and give ready-to-paste CSS. B fits 'basically no animation' better: it has only an instant default and an optional 100ms linear colour change. A adds a 200ms fade-in for overlays and a deceleration easing curve. A's black focus ring, chosen with contrast in mind, is a better call than B's tomato ring, but that doesn't outweigh B's tighter motion set. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers set radius to zero and show depth with rules and zero-blur offsets, but A fits 'basically no animation' more closely: transitions are instant by default, with one optional 100ms linear color change. B adds a 200ms duration for overlays appearing and a cubic-bezier easing, and its CSS draws 'raised' as a box-shadow spread while its table describes it as a border. A also states its exclusions and the decisions left to the user more clearly, though its optional 50% radius token slightly loosens the zero-radius rule.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep radius at zero with a circle exception, use borders and hard zero-blur offsets for depth, and keep motion close to instant while handling reduced motion. B is slightly better: its raised and overlay levels are distinct and come with clear reasons, it gives a complete CSS block including the reduced-motion media query, and it states its trade-offs and what it didn't check.
